---

\frametitle{Multiple predictors}

>- The coefficient $\beta_k$ is the average or expected difference in outcome y, comparing two people who
differ by one unit in the predictor $x_k$ while being equal in all the other predictors. This is sometimes
stated in shorthand as comparing two people (or, more generally, two observational units) that differ
in $x_k$ with all the other predictors held constant.

>- A one unit increase in $X$ is associated with a $\beta_x$ increase in $Y$, all else constant. 

---

\frametitle{Multiple predictors}

$$y_i=X_i+Z_i$$

I want to estimate the effect of $X$ on $Y$ conditional on $Z$ and I believe the effect of $X$ does not _depend_ on the level of $Z$. These effects are _independent_ of one another.

---

\frametitle{Multiple predictors}

$$y_i=X_i+Z_i+(X_i\times Z_i)$$

I want to estimate the effect of $X$ on $Y$ conditional on $Z$, but I also believe the effect of $X$ _depends_ on the level of $Z$. 

---

\frametitle{Multiple predictors}

>- What kind of hypotheses do interaction terms let me examine? What does an estimate of 0 on an interaction term mean?

>- \textbf{Interaction coefficient:} Tests whether the effect of $X$ is different across levels of $Z$.

\frametitle{Review}

\textbf{Research Question:} What is the average association between income and commute time across the twin cities, controlling for city? 

* $Y$ = commute time (continuous)
* $X$ = income (continuous)
* $Z$ = city (categorical: Minneapolis, St Paul)

\begin{align}
  &\textbf{A: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X) \\
  &\textbf{B: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X)+\beta_2(Z) \\
  &\textbf{C: } y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1(X)+\boxed{\beta_2}(Z) \\
  &\textbf{D: } y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1(X)+\beta_2(Z)+\boxed{\beta_3}(X \times Z) 
\end{align}

---

\frametitle{Review}

\textbf{Research Question:} Is the average association between income and commute time different depending on the city? 

* $Y$ = commute time (continuous)
* $X$ = income (continuous)
* $Z$ = city (categorical: Minneapolis, St Paul)

\begin{align}
  &\textbf{A: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X) \\
  &\textbf{B: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X)+\beta_2(Z) \\
  &\textbf{C: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X)+\beta_2(Z)+\beta_3(X \times Z) \\
  &\textbf{D: } y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1(X)+\beta_2(Z)+\boxed{\beta_3}(X \times Z) 
\end{align}

\frametitle{Review}

\textbf{What is the null hypothesis here?}

* $Y$ = commute time (continuous)
* $X$ = income (continuous)
* $Z$ = city (categorical: Minneapolis, St Paul)

\begin{align}
  &\textbf{A: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X) \\
  &\textbf{B: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X)+\beta_2(Z) \\
  &\textbf{C: } y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}(X)+\beta_2(Z)+\beta_3(X \times Z) \\
  &\textbf{D: } y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1(X)+\beta_2(Z)+\boxed{\beta_3}(X \times Z) 
\end{align}

$$y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1(\text{income})+\beta_2(\text{city=M})+\boxed{\beta_3}(\text{income} \times \text{city=SP})$$

---

$$y_i=10+3(\text{income})+20(\text{city=M})+\boxed{0}(\text{income} \times \text{city=SP})$$

>- What is the effect of income on commute time in Minneapolis?

\frametitle{Causal inference}

>- Transitioning to causal inference: How do I know if X has a _causal effect_ on Y?

---

\frametitle{Confounding}

>- I'm curious whether people who drink more wine live longer.

>- I do a huge survey where I follow people over time and track how much wine they drink and if they die.

>- I fit the regression model: $\text{mortality rate}=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{wine}$.

>- People who drink more wine are less likely to die (p<0.05)!

>- \textbf{Interpretation:} People who drank more wine are less likely to die _because_ they drank more wine; _if_ people drink more wine, _then_ they will be less likely to die. 

---

\frametitle{Confounding}

>- \textbf{Interpretation:} People who drank more wine are less likely to die _because_ they drank more wine; _if_ people drink more wine, _then_ they will be less likely to die. 

How might I get a coefficient estimate that is closer to this interpretation?

---

\frametitle{Confounding}

\small
$$\text{mortality rate}=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{wine}+\beta_2\text{age}+\beta_3\text{income}+\beta_4\text{education}+\beta_5\text{social}$$

>- People who drink more wine are less likely to die comparing within levels of age, income, education, and social networks (p<0.05)!

---

\frametitle{Confounding}

$$\text{mortality rate}=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{wine}$$

How might we avoid having to control for so many things? In other words, how might we guarantee the _only_ difference across our comparisons of drinking is the drinking?

---

\frametitle{DAGs}

Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are a way of graphically modelling our data generating process.

>- \textbf{Nodes:} random variables.

>- \textbf{Arrows:} causal effects between two nodes that move in the direction of the arrow.

---

\frametitle{DAGs}

		\draw [,->] (1) to (2);

	\end{tikzpicture}}

\end{figure}

---

\frametitle{DAGs}

Ground rules:

>- Causality runs in one direction: forward through time.

>- DAGs represent chains of events. 

>- DAGs operate in counterfactuals: use use them to compare hypothetical worlds, scenarios, interventions.

---

\frametitle{DAGs}

Why DAGs? 

>- Force you to think carefully about the logic of how different variables are related to each other.

>- Writing out a DAG prior to your analysis highlights the necessity of bringing in substantive, or domain, knowledge into your study.

\frametitle{Confounding}

In this case, if we are interested in the causal effect of wine on mortality, we would say that \textbf{income} acts as a \textbf{confounder}. Because income may have an effect on both wine drinking and mortality risk, the effect of wine estimated with a model not controlling for income would be at least partially spurious. 

\small
$$\text{mortality rate}=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{wine}+\beta_2\text{income}$$

\frametitle{Mediation}

>- \textbf{Mediators:} Variables along the causal pathway between our key treatment and the outcome. 

>- Mediators, mechanisms, etc.

\frametitle{Review}

1. Choose a functional form for the model.

2. Choose an estimator (i.e., objective function) that relates the model to real observed data (e.g., OLS).

3. Fit the model (e.g., estimate parameters) by optimizing the objective function.

---

\frametitle{Review}

1. Choose a functional form for the model.

$$y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}{x_i}+\epsilon_i$$

2. Choose an estimator (i.e., objective function) that relates the model to real observed data (e.g., OLS).

$$\text{Sum of squared residuals}=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\widehat{\beta_0}-\widehat{\beta_1}x_i)^2$$

3. Fit the model (e.g., estimate parameters) by optimizing the objective function.

---

\frametitle{Review}

1. Choose a functional form for the model.

$$y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}{x_i}+\epsilon_i$$

2. \textbf{We already know the best estimator for the linear model: OLS.}

3. \textbf{We already have pre-built R functions to fit the estimator to data.}

---

\frametitle{Review}

1. \textbf{We don't know the functional form for the model; we must justify our target comparison, or estimand, using theory.}

$$y_i=\beta_0+\boxed{\beta_1}{x_i}+\epsilon_i$$

2. We already know the best estimator for the linear model: OLS.

3. We already have pre-built R functions to fit the estimator to data.

\frametitle{DAGs}

How do I make a DAG?

>- \textbf{Simplify:} Only include nodes and arrows believed to represent important effects.
>- \textbf{Consolidate:} Search for nodes that are doing the same thing in your DAG. Consolidate into one node. 
>- \textbf{Mediators:} Are there certain variables that only exist as mediators? You can get rid of these unless you are specifically interested in their mediating effect. 
>- \textbf{Irrelevance:} Remove variables that are not on the causal pathway between your key treatment and outcome.

\frametitle{Confounding}

>- Do not listen to anyone who says "Well, you _have_ to control for X." 

>- What they are really saying: "The comparison in which you are not controlling for X is not useful; I'm assuming you want to make the comparison where you control for X." This can be an argument on theoretical grounds about the utility of various research questions.

>- There may be very good reasons to control for X! But it _completely_ depends on your research question; more specifically, exactly what \textbf{comparison} you say you're trying to make.

\frametitle{DAGs}

Key steps for building a quantitative research question:

>- \textbf{(1)} Draw a conceptual model to guide your research question.

>- \textbf{(2)} Read the literature. What do we know?

>- \textbf{(3)} Refine conceptual model into a DAG (this may include drawing the "causal field"). 

>- \textbf{(4)} Think systematically and explicitly about the potential effect of bias.
